thesis: Boise Cascade is earning a 1.64% net margin against a 6.79% five-year average while revenue per share is only 1.5% below last year, so this is a margin trough on intact volumes rather than a business in decline — and the balance sheet can wait it out, at 0.244 debt-to-equity, a 2.71 current ratio and $15.85 of cash flow per share against $2.94 of EPS. Normalizing that margin on $183.32 of revenue per share gives $12.45 of earnings power, which at a mid-cycle 10x supports $124.50 against a $77.74 price of 1.35x book.
key_risk: The concrete invalidation, since a long-term accumulation carries no stop: gross margin failing to recover above 18% for two consecutive quarters, or revenue per share turning down more than 5% year over year — that would mean the trough is structural rather than cyclical and the 6.79% five-year average margin is no longer the right normal. The near-term danger is different: mortgage rates track the 10Y, and the same 35bp rally that just lifted homebuilders reverses if the December hike drags the long end up.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that the whole idea rests on one assumption — the multiple. At 10x normalized earnings the reward-to-risk is 2.59 and clears the floor; at 9x the target is $112 and it is 1.92 and FAILS. So this publishes on a mid-cycle multiple being the right multiple, and a cyclical that stays at trough margins deserves a trough multiple, not a mid-cycle one. I am not claiming to have resolved that, which is why the scale plan takes a third at 88.43 and another third at the conservative 8x figure of 99.60 — most of the realisable return does not require the full 124.50, and the position is 3% rather than a core holding.

evidence.detail: Method shown: revenue per share TTM $183.32 x five-year average net profit margin 6.79% = $12.45 normalized EPS; at a mid-cycle 10x that is $124.50 (8x = $99.60, 12x = $149.40). Bear case set at book value per share of $57.99, supported by 0.244 debt/equity, a 2.71 current ratio and $15.85 cash flow per share. Current margin 1.64% vs the 6.79% average is the gap being bought.

thesis: Huntington Ingalls is a growing defence business that has de-rated on multiple rather than on earnings: revenue is up 13.97% and EPS up 25.70% over the trailing year, net margin is 5.01% against a 5.34% five-year average, and the stock is still 33.8% below its 460.00 52-week high at 16.6x trailing earnings. key_risk: The concrete invalidation: two consecutive quarters of shipbuilding margin below the prior year, or a submarine build-rate slip or appropriation cut. Margin erosion on fixed-price Navy work is this company documented failure mode and five-year EPS growth is -1.94%, so the flat-earnings path is the base case the bear price of 210.00 reflects, not a tail.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is now arithmetic rather than narrative, and it is mine: on honestly derived anchors this idea returns 2.15 and FAILS the 2.5 long-term floor. The ratio spans 1.81 to 5.25 across defensible multiple and bear-case choices, which means the levels are not well-founded in either direction and the previous 430.00 target with a 230.00 bear case was flattering rather than informative — the bear case sat 12.2% below entry on a stock that had already fallen 44%. I have not answered this; I have measured it, and the consequence is that the position is held and trimmed rather than built.

catalyst.event: Q3 earnings 2026-11-03, verified on the fetched finnhub calendar. The driver is not the print: it is net margin recovering from 6.80% toward the 17.33% five-year average on revenue that is already flat.
catalyst.action: HOLD, no adds at 30.03. Build the remaining tranches only under 28.50. The number to read in the release is operating expense and margin, not revenue — gross margin is already above its five-year average, so the problem is below the gross line.

thesis: Pfizer earns a 6.80% net margin against a 17.33% five-year average on revenue that is essentially flat year over year at -0.22%, so the de-rating is a margin and opex story rather than a demand collapse — and gross margin at 74.71% is actually ABOVE its 69.76% five-year average, which locates the problem below the gross line rather than in pricing power. Normalizing that margin on $11.18 of revenue per share gives $1.94 of earnings power, against which the 30.03 price is 15.5x and the 42.00 target is 21.7x, while a 5.38% dividend yield pays for the holding period.
key_risk: The concrete invalidation, since a long-term accumulation carries no stop: two consecutive quarters of declining non-COVID product revenue, or a late-stage pipeline failure in the assets the re-rating depends on. Note what is NOT the invalidation — a falling price. The genuine structural danger is that the patent cliff makes the 17.33% five-year average margin the wrong normal, in which case normalized EPS is well below $1.94 and the whole anchor moves.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that cheap pharma has been a value trap for years and a patent cliff is an arithmetic loss of earnings power rather than a sentiment problem, so normalizing to a five-year average margin that includes COVID-era windfalls overstates the normal. That objection is partly answered and partly conceded: it is answered by the gross margin being above its five-year average, which shows pricing and mix are not the problem, and by revenue being flat rather than falling; it is conceded in the downside, which is why the bear case was deliberately lowered to 23.26 and the ratio still clears the floor at 3.32 rather than the flattering 4.65 the old number gave.

evidence.detail: Method shown: revenue per share TTM $11.18 x five-year average net margin 17.33% = $1.94 normalized EPS; spot 30.03 is 15.5x that and the 42.00 target is 21.7x. Bear case 23.26 = 12x normalized, essentially the 23.62 52-week low. Normalized P/E 22.03 against a trailing 39.51 shows the gap.
